the *Tuṣita* devas, one by one, emanate from every pore clouds of exquisite flower and incense canopies equal in number to the realms of sentient beings, as offerings to Śākyamuni Buddha.
As soon as this devaputra had scattered the fragrant flowers, within each flower he beheld all the Tathāgatas.
At that time, those clouds of incense universally perfumed the sentient beings in worlds as numerous as the atoms of immeasurable Buddha-fields.
Those who smell its fragrance will have all eighty-four thousand afflictions and karmic obstructions completely extinguished,
becoming fully endowed with the roots of goodness of sovereign radiance.
Those who see it plant the roots of goodness of a single Ganges-sand number of universal wheel-turning kings.
As explained at length in the sūtras.
Question:
Why is this benefit called "transmitting and communicating to accomplish inexhaustible practice"?
Answer:
Upon seeing the flowers, incense, and canopies offered by the first devaputra, he perceived that each successive offering yielded inexhaustible benefits.
Then, within each individual flower offered by the second devaputra, he beheld all the Tathāgatas.
Sentient beings as numerous as atoms receive the benefit of extinguishing their hindrances through the incense offered by this son of heaven.

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who, upon seeing the cloud-like canopy offered by this son of heaven, plant roots of goodness for becoming a wheel-turning monarch as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River.
This wheel-turning king emits the sovereign light of the *mandārava* flower;
all sentient beings who encounter this radiance attain the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of a bodhisattva.
This wheel-turning king also emits the light of the *cūḍāmaṇi* jewel.
All who see it attain the ten stages of a bodhisattva;
they all obtain the immeasurable light of wisdom and attain the samādhi of the accomplishment of pure power through the sixteen faculties.
This means that through the power of a single secondary characteristic (*anulakṣaṇa*) and a single light, these immeasurable practices are transmitted and accomplished;
the same applies to the other characteristics and lights.
Therefore, the Commentary states:
By this, one may infer that these are all the power of a single ray of light within one of the Tathāgata’s minor marks.
If it is so for one ray, it is likewise so for all the other rays.
As it is with one minor mark,
so it is with the remaining minor marks;
as it is with the minor marks, so it is with all of them.
The remaining great marks, such as the oceans and so forth, are unspeakably unspeakable.
Such is the meaning of the text;
reflect upon this.
The statement that all sentient beings in the world have previously cultivated goodness clarifies that they possess,
from former lives, the vision and hearing of the One Vehicle,
and have thus cultivated the roots of goodness of Samantabhadra.
Question:
What is the status of those who hold the position of a wheel-turning monarch as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River? Answer: [The state of] a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*).
Regarding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*),
the commentary states:
"The fragrant flowers, canopies, and other offerings emitted from the pores of this devaputra further benefit sentient beings."
Causing others to attain the status of a Wheel-Turning King is also [the fruit of] the tenth stage.
Question:
Why does it not say "two times as many as the sands of the Ganges" for the Wheel-Turning Kings, but rather "one time as many as the sands of the Ganges"?
Answer:
The commentary states:
"The first clarifies the general overview of this dharma-gate for perceiving this dharma-realm."
Thus, one obtains the roots of goodness of a wheel-turning monarch (cakravartin) as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
all like the pure white jewel net and so forth;
these are the wheel-turning monarchs among the ten thousand sons within the nature of this world-system.
Such as King Subhāṣita, King of Loving Vision, and others;
they were not like the thousand-soned Cakravartin kings of the four continents with golden wheels,
but rather Cakravartin kings of pure white jewel nets as numerous as the sands of one Ganges River.
By merely seeing this canopy, one’s roots of goodness are suddenly brought to fulfillment.
Regarding the third, Sudhana: as for the name "Sudhana," it is established because his physical appearance is characterized by the wealth and treasures resulting from these meritorious rewards.
Thus, goodness is the cause and wealth is the fruit.
Furthermore, because one obtains this wealth that accords with the Path, it is called "Good Wealth" (Sudhana).
Moreover, at the time of birth, jewels appeared as his wealth.
Later, he praised his conduct and virtue as being excellent,
like those such as Subhūti and Śūnyatā-sambhava.
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the name of Sadāprarudita and so forth.
Based on this, it may be understood.
Within the second section, which praises his virtuous conduct, there are ten phrases arranged in five pairs.
The first pair concerns how he once made offerings to the Buddhas and planted roots of goodness.
This clarifies that Sudhana has already planted the roots of merit conducive to liberation (*mokṣabhāgīya-kuśalamūla*) in previous lives.
Second, he delights in purity and draws near to spiritual friends; third, he cultivates the three types of action (*trikarma*);
fourth, he seeks the dharmas that are the fruits of such cultivation.
The fifth is the purity of mind through complete practice.
Because the mind is free from divergent thoughts, it is pure like space;
furthermore, because there are no manifest afflictions and the like, this is the text from the *Shu* (Commentary), fascicle 18.
Question:
Is this youth a prince or the son of a householder? Answer: [He is a prince.]
The sutra text merely states that there were five hundred youths,
such as Sudhana, and does not clarify their parents;
however, judging by the fact that there were seven great treasuries within his residence, he must have been the son of a wealthy elder.
Since it is not stated that he was within the palace, he was not a prince.
Nevertheless, because he had already brought forth the seven treasures,
the *Kongmoku* and other texts describe him as a "superior person" (*śreṣṭha*) of Jambudvīpa.
Question:
Why does this youth seek a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), while others do not?
Answer:
Because this person possesses past roots of goodness,
and because they now also seek out virtuous friends.
The Sūtra says:
"This youth has already made offerings to the Buddhas of the past and has deeply planted roots of goodness;
he constantly delights in purity and draws near to virtuous friends."
Purifying body, speech, and mind, one cultivates the bodhisattva path and seeks all-knowledge.
Question:
Mañjuśrī instructed him to seek virtuous friends.
If there is something to be indicated,
the answer is:
the commentary states that there are seven.
First, because it serves as a model;
that is, it is the model for seeking the Dharma and teaching the Dharma.
Second, because its objective conditions for practice are superior.
That is to say, in the essentials for accomplishing practice, there is nothing that does not take a virtuous friend as primary.
This is because it increases the destruction of the three [types of] views;
it causes novice Bodhisattvas such as Sudhana to destroy their own arrogance and the views resulting from [past] retribution.
Fourth, because it establishes the practice by relying [on others]:
namely, the practice of seeking virtuous friends and the practice of seeking the Dharma.
Fifth, because it manifests the stages by relying [on them].
Extensively entrusting this to spiritual friends reveals the five stages beginning with faith;
it manifests their profundity and vastness,
and symbolizes the profundity and vastness of the Buddha-dharma.
Although his rank was supreme, he declared, "I know only this single Dharma-gate.
When Sudhana established his seat and ascended it, he said,
"I do not yet know how the bodhisattva practices are performed," and so forth.
Seventh, because it manifests dependent origination:
Sudhana and his spiritual friend together constitute a single dependent origination,
for there is no duality between the one who enters and that which is entered.
Therefore, there is no Sudhana outside of the Good Friends;
thus, it is manifested that the one is all,
clarifying how Sudhana traverses the various stages.
Since there is no virtuous friend external to Sudhana,
this reveals that all things are one, demonstrating that the various stages are established within Sudhana himself.
Question:
What is the meaning of "virtuous friend"?
Answer:
There are three categories.
First, the person;
second, the dharma;
third, the combined discernment.
In the beginning, there are six [points].
First, there are those who, though able to relieve suffering, do not encourage the cultivation of goodness;
such persons are not true spiritual friends.
Second, although they encourage the cultivation of worldly virtues so as to avoid the evil realms, they do not encourage [them] to turn toward the supramundane;
such persons are also not true friends.
Third, although they cultivate both types of practice, they do not encourage the path of the bodhisattva.
Fourth, although one cultivates the bodhisattva path, one still retains the perception of signs;
fifth, one must exhort sentient beings to practice signless conduct to be a true spiritual friend;
sixth, one must exhort them to fulfill the practices of Samantabhadra before becoming a truly ultimate spiritual friend.
The two dharmas of the spiritual friend also have six layers:
first, the dharma of humans and devas;
second, the dharma of the Two Vehicles.
Third, the teaching of the beginning;
fourth, the teaching of the end;
fifth, the sudden teaching.
Sixth, the teaching of the perfect circle:
because one accomplishes correct practice by relying on these teachings,
they are called "virtuous friends."
Within the "Discernment of the Three Unifications" (Sanhe Bian), there are likewise six layers.
For each of the dharmas in the aforementioned six positions, one gate is explained;
by thus imparting [the teaching] to those with the appropriate capacity, both person and dharma are discerned together.
Second, the specific analysis of the subsequent text:
All spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) possess the aforementioned three [qualities].
Within these three stages, each possesses the three meanings.
As stated in the Commentary (Sū) 18.
However, there are differing accounts regarding the number of spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra),
as explained in the original text of the Commentary 18 and in the *Gāngmù* (Outline).
Question:
Based on this boy, how are the three births distinguished?
Answer: [As follows:]
According to the school of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), there are three stages.
The first is the stage of seeing and hearing,
which corresponds to the body of Sudhana’s birth immediately preceding the present one.
Because they have seen and heard such teachings of Samantabhadra,
and because they have accomplished those roots of goodness conducive to liberation,
the text praising their virtues says:
This youth has already made offerings to the Buddhas of the past and has deeply planted roots of goodness.

Furthermore, the thirty-seventh passage of the *Xingqi pin* (Chapter on the Arising of Nature) asks: "How does a bodhisattva know and see the roots of goodness planted by what the Tathāgata sees, hears, honors, and makes offerings to?"
The roots of goodness of this bodhisattva are entirely unfailing;
his merit is inexhaustible;
he is free from all craving and has attained ultimate liberation.
The retribution is not in vain;
it fulfills all aspirations and is inexhaustible within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

Only when the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) manifests does one finally attain the karma for cultivating the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) over the course of a hundred kalpas, a thousand kalpas,
or as many kalpas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges.
Sixth, with respect to the final stage of the body within the cycle of birth and death,
one immediately becomes a Buddha.
As the lower fascicle states:
If one follows the Hīnayāna, there is only the body of segmented existence;
even upon reaching the ultimate stage,
the Buddha remains the same.
This is real and not a transformation.
Seventh, based on the twelve stages (*vihāra*) of the Hīnayāna,
the twelfth— the stage of the supreme Arhat— is identical to that of a Buddha.
The lower fascicle states:
"In all the teachings, they are briefly indicated by means of three meanings.
The first is to clarify the characteristics of the stages."
Second, the explanation of non-retrogression;
third, the clarification of the aspects of practice.
Regarding the first, according to the Hīnayāna, there are four stages.
This refers to the stages of expedient means, vision, cultivation,
and the ultimate. Furthermore, it is taught that the twelve abodes of the Hīnayāna constitute the ultimate for those who do not regress.
This is because one attains non-retrogression upon reaching the stage of patience (*kṣānti*) through this practice.
Its specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are also as described in those various treatises.
The *Zhongnan Wenda* states:
If one relies on the teachings of the Hīnayāna and perceives the Buddha’s physical body with its thirty-two marks and so forth,
this is indeed seeing the eye faculty in simultaneous correspondence with its object;
seeing these actual physical characteristics is called "seeing the Buddha."
In the Hīnayāna, there are two types of Buddhas:
first, the birth-body (janma-kāya);
second, the transformation-body (nirmāṇa-kāya).
The Buddha has perfected the practice of compassion and loving-kindness through simultaneous cultivation;
at one and the same time,
it is solely the Bodhisattva who possesses this practice of compassion and loving-kindness.
One becomes a Buddha by following the sequence of the thirty-three minds;
other practitioners do not become Buddhas,
but merely attain two kinds of nirvana and abide in the realm of no-remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa).
Only a single person attains Buddhahood;
if other persons were to attain Buddhahood, their times—whether before or after—would not coincide.
This is so regarding the transformation of sentient beings.
In a later time, he will become a Buddha;
because there are no Buddhas in the ten directions,
this refers to the great eons (*mahākalpa*) of the formation and destruction of the world-system.
One must complete three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* to definitely attain Buddhahood.
There is not a single instance of attaining Buddhahood in a single thought-moment, nor is there a Buddha in another land;
even if such a thing were to exist, [it would be impossible].
This refers to the Buddha of this world traveling to that other realm through transformation.
Māyā, the mother of the Buddha, is the actual mother here in Jambudvīpa;
in other worlds, there is no such actual mother.
Because the Buddha is an emanation, the Buddha,
Bodhisattvas, and others manifest through the characteristics of their various faculties;
these are merely produced as transformations and do not involve a modification of their fundamental nature.
One person, relying on one person, relying on one realm, and relying on one mind, successively attains Buddhahood.
The correspondence between cause and effect is such that it can be known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
There is, however, a distinction based on whether the causes and effects for severing delusions are fully exhausted or not.
The various factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*) constitute the general retributive karma;
from the initial generation of the mind of awakening, one practices them in successive order until the point of attaining Buddhahood.
During the final moments of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), for a period of one hundred eons, one separately cultivates the karma for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
This is real and not a transformation;
however, by practicing the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma),
those who might otherwise regress shall all become Buddhas, and there shall be none who do not attain Buddhahood.
Taking the human form as the Buddha,
while all-encompassing wisdom and so forth belong to the Dharma.
The fifth fascicle of the *Wǔjiào* (Five Teachings) states:
If categorized according to the lineage (*gotra*) of the Hīnayāna, there are six types:
namely, those subject to regression, those who reflect, those who guard, those who abide, those who advance, and the immovable.
Within the immovable lineage, there are three grades.
The superior, middling, and inferior correspond respectively to those of the three vehicles.
Although it is stated herein that only the Buddha alone possesses the lineage (gotra),
this does not refer to the nature of that great enlightenment (mahābodhi).
Because it does not describe the Buddha’s qualities as being exhausted even until the end of the future, nor the arising of his great activity and so forth;
therefore, one should know that within this teaching:
Except for the Buddha alone, it is said that all other sentient beings do not possess the nature of great bodhi.
Third, regarding the teaching gate of the initial turning of the mind, there are eight meanings.
First, in terms of the stages of realization (*bhūmi*),
there are the ten stages beginning with the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*);
within the tenth stage, one attains Buddhahood.

The reason why [the sūtra] states that they attain Buddhahood at the same time as those in the tenth stage is that the Buddha intentionally aligns himself with the causal stages; thus he makes this statement.
The Record says:
The *Fajing lun* states:
"It leads the small mind to develop great practice;
it causes the fear of life to be forgotten and discarded, thereby maintaining liberation."
The commentary states:
The intent behind establishing the ten stages, beginning with the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśana-bhūmi),
is to cause one to abandon the understanding and guarding characteristic of the Hīnayāna.
This is because one enters into the Mahāyāna.
Question:
If that is so, for what purpose are the stages such as the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśana-bhūmi) established?
Answer:
Because the realization and understanding of emptiness has not yet been accomplished,
one does not allow them to be made sharp, as they remain at the stage of dry wisdom (śuklavidarśana-bhūmi).
This means that the moisture of the principle of emptiness is like water;
therefore, only by awakening to emptiness can the mind of wisdom increase.
Second is the Stage of Nature (Gotrabhūmi).
Because of the understanding of emptiness,
one uses this understanding to subdue the fetters;
since this understanding is firm and unchanging, it is called the "Stage of Nature" (dharmatā-bhūmi).
Regarding the "ground of the eight persons":
because one understands the four truths in both their true and apparent aspects,
and since there are two types of persons for each of the four truths, the eight patiences (*kṣānti*) are called the ground of the eight persons.
Within each of the Truths there are two types of patience (*kṣānti*):
thus, within the Truth of Suffering of the Desire Realm, there is the Patience of Suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*),
and within the Truth of Suffering of the two upper realms, there is the Subsequent Patience of Suffering (*duḥkha-anvaya-kṣānti*).
The remaining three truths are to be understood by analogy with this.
The eight patiences (*kṣānti*) are rare because they are immediately followed [by the fruits].
These eight factors induced by the eight patiences are the eight liberations (*vimokṣa*).
Regarding the fourth, the stage of seeing (*darśana-bhūmi*):
by means of these eight patiences (*kṣānti*), one attains the eight stages;
because the sixteenth moment of mind is fulfilled, one perceives the principle of the equality of the four truths.
Therefore, it is called the "ground of seeing" (*darśana-bhūmi*).
As for the fifth, the "ground of thinning" (*tanu-bhūmi*):
from the ground of seeing, one gives rise to the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga-jñāna*).
Among the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm, one has severed the first six grades while halting at the final three; therefore,
it is called the Stage of Thinness (tanubhūmi).
Regarding the "six stages of freedom from desire":
because the final three grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation have been completely exhausted, one does not return to the desire realm;
therefore, they are called the stages of freedom from desire.
Regarding the seventh, the stage of the "accomplished" (kṛtāvibhūmi):
because the fetters of the three realms have been completely exhausted, one attains the fruit of arhatship;
therefore, it is called the stage of the accomplished.
The [remaining] three stages can be understood [by this].
The above summarizes the intent of the *Dharmādarśa-śāstra*.
Question:
The ten stages, beginning with the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*), are practiced in common by the three vehicles. Why, then,
are these ten stages taught at the very beginning of this chapter within the teaching on the transformation of the mind?
Within the *Fifty Essential Questions and Answers*,
first the causes and effects of the six realms of existence are established;
next, the two vehicles of the ignorant dharma are elucidated.
Next, the Buddhas of the Hīnayāna and those of the Hīnayāna who have turned their minds [toward the Mahāyāna] are explained.
Next, the Buddhas of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) at the stage of the fulfillment of the five ranks are explained.
However, the ten stages, beginning with the Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-vipaśyanā), are established.
Finally, he established the seventeen sequential gates for the Bodhisattva Ṛjuvartin.
The reply states:
"The Mirror of Wisdom Virtue says:"
This establishes the foundation for ascending through the ten stages (bhūmis) practiced in common by the three vehicles (triyāna).
This teaching is the standard established by Master [Fashao].
That master explained it according to the stages through three successive cycles.
That is to say: first, explaining the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the distinct teachings of the three vehicles;
second, reconciling the ten stages of the distinct teachings with the stages of the common teaching;
and third, reconciling the ten stages of the common teaching.
Within the stage of penetrating the source,
if one relies on the initial stage,

the "Stage of Dry Wisdom" is explained within the vicinity of the final stage of the ordinary person (bālapṛthagjana), characterized by the nature of emptiness; it is at this point that the five contemplations for settling the mind (pañca-samatha-vastūni) may be practiced.
The stage of the nature of the ground (*gotrabhūmi*) refers to the stage of general mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*), the stage of specific mindfulness of the body,
and its conjunction with the four wholesome faculties; these constitute the five stages of skillful means.
This constitutes the stage of the nature of the ground (*gotrabhūmi*).
Within these five preliminary practices (*upāya*), there are both general and specific aspects;
in two of the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), one equally contemplates the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
In the latter four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), the method for contemplating the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*) is distinguished;
therefore, the two applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), general and specific, are combined into one.
As for the stage of the person of eightfold knowledge (*aṣṭamaka-bhūmi*):
"Abiding in the stage of patience regarding suffering" refers to abiding in the stage of the path of seeing as a *srotāpanna*.
"The ground of vision" refers to abiding in the stage of the path of seeing as a *srotāpanna*.
The "Stage of Thinness" refers to being established in the stage of the Sakṛdāgāmin.
The "Stage of Freedom from Desire" refers to...
One established in the stage of *anāgāmin* is so called;
one established in the stage of "having accomplished what was to be done" (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*) is established in the stage of *arhat*.
These seven stages belong to the Śrāvaka vehicle;
as for the stage of the Pratyekabuddha:
This can be understood.
Regarding the stages of a bodhisattva,
these thirty mental states (triṃśac-citta) are not yet explained within this Separate Teaching (pratyeka-vidhi).
This refers exclusively to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Among the four types of bodhisattvas, the first stage is called the stage of those who have newly resolved their minds (*navayānasaṃprasthita-bhūmi*).
This includes the second stage through the sixth stage.
The stages from the seventh dwelling to the ninth dwelling are called the stage of the long-practiced path.
They are also called the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
The tenth dwelling is called the stage of being "born once more to attain buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
The further state of perfect awakening at the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*) is not mentioned here,
as the tenth dwelling is taken as the conclusion.
This is precisely the realization of the True Buddha with the physical form of sixteen feet.
As for the second category,
the Buddha of the Separate Teaching is the Buddha who conceals his traces.
Therefore, they are relegated to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*),
so that they may enter those ten stages of faith.
As for the five fruits of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*):
This establishes [the practitioner] prior to the ten faiths,
causing them to enter the stage of the ten faiths.
Question:
If that is so, why do the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha) not abide in the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) despite being in the initial mind of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*)?
The *Renwang jing* states:
Since the initial mind of the stage of practicing the seeds (śikṣā-bīja) has already transcended the two vehicles,
it is known that one does not yet abide in the ten abodes (daśa-vihāra).

The stages of nature (dharmatā-bhūmi) and the ground of dry wisdom (śuṣka-jñāna-bhūmi) described within the five expedient means are both regressed and placed within the ordinary stage prior to faith.

It is thus: although the Separate Teaching (Pṛthagvidyā) posits ten stages (*bhūmi*), it establishes these ten stages as common to the three vehicles (*triyāna*) in order to cause [practitioners] to enter the Shared Teaching (Sāmānyavidyā).
Since this is the Shared Teaching (tongjiao),
one only then comes to know that the Buddha-way is long and distant,
and that one must pass through the three stages of worthiness (sanhuan) and the ten stages of the bodhisattva (shidi) before practicing until finally attaining Buddhahood.
Therefore, within the ten stages of faith of the Shared Teaching, there are five grades of disciples;
that is to say, the four fruits of the śrāvaka and the fruit of the pratyekabuddha constitute these five.
Question:
If that is so, how are the four stages of a bodhisattva to be understood?
Answer:
The stage of the seeds of practice corresponds to the bodhisattva who has newly resolved [to attain enlightenment].
Those of the nature-seed lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*) and the path-seed lineage (*mārga-gotra*) are those who have practiced the path for a long time.

From the first stage (*bhūmi*) upward, they are all those who are non-retrogressive (*avaivartika*). Equal-enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) refers to those in their final birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
Sublime enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*) refers to the Bodhisattva.
Question:
By means of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao), one integrates the Distinct Teaching (biejiao);
having integrated the Distinct Teaching, one provisionally establishes the stages of the Distinct Teaching by conforming them to those of the Shared Teaching.
How is it that, according to the direct teaching of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), the three vehicles practice the ten stages together?
Answer:
The five fruits of the two vehicles are integrated into the stage of the ten faiths within the Shared Teaching.
It is called the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*).
The stage of the Three Worthies (*trividha-ārya*) is the Stage of Nature (*gotra-bhūmi*).
Within the first eight stages, the proximate means are called the Stage of the Eight Patiences (*aṣṭakṣānti-bhūmi*).
The first stage is called the Stage of Vision (*darśana-bhūmi*).
The second stage is that of the Once-Returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*), called the Stage of Thinning (*tanu-bhūmi*).
The third and fourth stages are called the Stage of Freedom from Desire (*vītarāga-bhūmi*).
The fifth stage corresponds with the contemplation of the truths;
therefore, it is called the stage of the Arhat who has accomplished what was to be done.
The sixth stage is the contemplation of causes and conditions.
Therefore, it is called the stage of the Pratyekabuddha;
reaching Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi) is called the stage of the Bodhisattva;
and Wondrous Enlightenment (miao-jue) is called the stage of the Buddha.
The third type is one who,
having severed the obstacles and afflictions of the Shared Teaching (p’ung-chiao) until they are exhausted,
still regresses from the Buddha-fruition they have attained.
They are settled within the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Shared Doctrine (*pāryāyika*).

Those who regress from the ten stages (*bhūmi*) of the Shared Teaching are settled within the five ranks of disciples (*pañca-vidha-śrāvaka*) at the stage of the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*) of the Shared Doctrine;
this refers to the stage of the *srotāpanna*, which includes both the path and the fruit.
Therefore, they correspond respectively to the first two abodes.
Up to the fifth grade of disciple, who is named a *pratyekabuddha*;
this [grade] likewise possesses both the path and the fruit.
Therefore, based on the ninth and twelfth stages [of the Bodhisattva path],
a question is asked:
If that is so, why is the fruit of Buddhahood established within the "fulfillment of the ten faiths" (daśa-śraddhā-paripūri) of the General Vehicle (sāmānya-yāna)?
The ten stages of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao) correspond to the ten abodes (shizhu) for disciples of the five grades.
Answer:
This is based on the actual [status of] the five grades.
The disciple and the Buddha do not possess distinct continuums; rather,
by relying solely on the Shared Teaching (pāṭha-sāmānya), they reach the stage of Buddhahood within that teaching,
thereby regaining faith and fulfilling the mind of conviction.
Therefore, when the Buddha actually regresses, his nature also regresses;
this is established as being the same for the five grades of disciples.
Consequently, such a person truly regresses from the Buddha who is full of faith.
When these are renamed as the complete cultivation of the ten stages of faith, they constitute the śrāvakas;
furthermore, they constitute the bodhisattvas of the ten abidings.
This can be understood through careful reflection.
Question:
If that is so, why is it that, in the context of the Buddha of the Shared Teaching (pāryāyika-yāna), one establishes the fulfillment of faith within the [stages of] the Bodhisattva,
yet only those of the Distinct Teaching (pratiniyata-yāna) are directed to cultivate the ten stages of practice (daśabhūmi-vihāra)?
Furthermore, he does not require them to cultivate the ten stages of faith (śraddhā) of the Penetrating School (Tongzong).
Answer:
That vehicle’s teaching is not a true exposition.

Only by penetrating the fundamental principle (tongzong) can one attain the realization; at that time, regarding the fruit of Buddhahood, one immediately attains faith in the penetration of the fundamental principle.
Therefore, the vehicle of the fruit of Buddhahood and the faith in the penetration of the fundamental principle are identical.
This is like when one gives rise to the faith of the One Vehicle within the first stage (bhūmi); at that very moment, the faith of the One Vehicle is perfected within that first stage.
Question:
For what reason do those of the Separate Teaching (Bie-jiao) among the three vehicles further cultivate the faith of the Shared Teaching (Tong-jiao)?
Answer:
That teaching states that Buddhahood is attained through thirty-four moments of thought;
it explains this matter in its entirety.
Because there is faith in the true Buddha, that person truly becomes a Buddha and is further led to cultivate the faith of the Universal Teaching (Pāramitā-yāna).
Because no one believes in this matter, there are none who have reached the fruit of Buddhahood through the Distinct Teaching;
therefore, they are further led to cultivate Mahāyāna faith.
Question:
Question: "The 'Pervasive Principle' (Tongzong) is superior to that school; one should further cultivate this practice.
Answer:
"Among the ten levels of faith (shixin), the first five are the five faculties (pañcendriya), such as faith and the rest."
In establishing the five mental states based on the meaning of these five faculties,
although they possess the complete substance of the dharmas in reality,
this applies to practitioners of the Shared Teaching.
One possesses the five faculties of the mundane world, such as faith and so forth, all at once;
if one has not yet possessed these five faculties, [one does not possess them].
A practitioner who proceeds directly will take ten thousand kalpas before they can cultivate the practice of the ten faiths and achieve this state of faith.
Question:
If that is so, since those of the three vehicles according to the distinct teaching possess the five supramundane faculties of the Hīnayāna,
they should achieve the faculty of faith immediately upon being subsumed by the Shared Teaching.
Answer:
The faculties (indriya) of the Hīnayāna and the Mahāyāna are not different.
Question:
If this is so, when these five classes of disciples practice the ten stages of dwelling (daśavihāra), [what occurs]?
For what reason is the name "śrāvaka" (disciple) given?
Answer:
Because this person practices by means of the transmitted teachings and doctrines.
Because they are śrāvakas who initiate practice upon hearing the sound [of the Dharma],
they are designated as "śrāvaka disciples" based on this meaning. However,
if one considers only the sense of understanding the principle of the single true mind, [they would not be so called].
This refers to the Bodhisattva of the Ten Faiths.
Since one attains Buddhahood once the obstructions and defilements have been severed,
why is it that [the practitioner] regresses and settles back into the initial stage of the Ten Faiths within the General Vehicle (Tongzong)?
Answer:
The Buddha-fruit you have established is merely a transformation Buddha emanated during the eight phases of attaining enlightenment within my stage of the ten faiths.
In order that they may realize the true Buddha, he causes them to retreat and practice.
Question:
If this is so, how does it accord with the sequence of the doctrinal systems?
What is the form and appearance of the common practice of the three vehicles?
Answer:
A person on the stage of srotāpanna performs the five preparatory practices (pañca-pūrvamgama-prayoga).
This constitutes the three stages of the ten faiths;
as the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* states:
"The ten faiths are divided into three grades."
That is to say: first, the inferior grade constitutes the stage of dry wisdom;
second, the middling grade constitutes the stage of following faith;
and third, the superior grade constitutes the stage of practice through the Dharma.
That which is of medium and superior grade is called the Stage of Nature (*gotrabhūmi*).
The next two dwellings constitute the Stage of Thinning (*tanubhūmi*,
referring to the third and fourth dwellings).
Up to the tenth stage constitutes the level of a pratyekabuddha.
If one follows the sequence of stages,
the nature-seed (prakṛti-gotra) corresponds to those who have newly resolved their minds [to attain awakening].
The lineage of the path (*mārga-jāti*) constitutes long-term practice;
those from the first bhūmi upward are *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive);
and those at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) are those in their final birth (*ekajāti-pratibaddha*).
Sublime Awakening constitutes the stage of Buddhahood.
If one follows the general school (zītōng zōng),
the ten stages of faith constitute the level of external ordinary beings.
Therefore, the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) and the stage of the cultivated seeds (*vāsanā-bīja*) both encompass these two [approaches].
That is to say, for those who enter via the sudden teaching (*tun-jiao*),
five grades of disciples are established.
The principle of the stages of the hidden Bodhisattva is such that the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) constitute the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā-bhūmi*),
because the two stages of the nature-lineage (*prakṛti-gotra*) and the cultivation-lineage (*paripuṣṭa-gotra*) serve as the proximate preparations for entering the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
It constitutes the ground of the eight patiences (*kṣānti*).
The first, second, and third grounds consist of the patience of faith (*śraddhā-kṣānti*);
therefore, the *srotāpanna* is called the "ground of vision" (*darśana-bhūmi*).
The fourth, fifth, and sixth stages constitute the stage of compliance with patience;
therefore, the *sakṛdāgāmin* is called the "stage of attenuation.
The seventh, eighth, and ninth stages constitute the stage of non-arising patience.
Therefore, the Anāgāmin is called the stage of freedom from desire.
The tenth stage is the patience of cessation;
because it is of inferior grade, the Arhat is called the stage of having accomplished what was to be done.
Samyaksambodhi is designated as the stage of the Pratyekabuddha;
the preceding stages collectively are termed the Bodhisattva stages;
and Subtle Enlightenment is termed the Buddha stage.
The above summarizes the intent of Master Fajinglun;
according to the intent of Upādhyāya Yan, that master’s doctrine consists of three levels of teaching.
These refer to the ten stages (daśabhūmi) practiced in common by the three vehicles.
The disciples do not possess the Perfect Teaching. Why is this?
It is because those of the Two Vehicles are not called "those who enter the One Vehicle."
Furthermore, within the Hīnayāna, only Śākyamuni Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, while all others do not;
thus, they do not establish the ten stages of common practice (*sādhāraṇa-bhūmi*). As for the establishment of the ten stages of common practice:
The intention is to lead all followers of the Hīnayāna into the Mahāyāna;
therefore, the meaning of the questions and answers is the same, and it does not establish the category of the ten shared stages (*bhūmi*).
Consequently, it first clarifies the Hīnayāna and the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
The principle of "turning the mind" (*huixin*) throughout the three teachings of Initial, Final, and Sudden constitutes the first [section].
The principle of "direct advancement" (*zhijin*) throughout the three teachings of Initial, Final, and Sudden constitutes the second [section].
Now, the intent of this chapter, while in substance it encompasses the Final Teaching, is primarily concerned with the Sudden Teaching.
However, based on the initial turning of the mind toward awakening, the ten stages such as the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*) are explained.
In the Sudden Teaching (*tun-jiao*), there are ten stages common to the practice of the three vehicles,
yet the distinct sequence of their respective positions is not clarified.
Therefore, the ten stages common to the three vehicles are not employed here.
Question:
If that is so, why does the commentary further establish the ten stages—such as the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*)—within the Sudden Teaching?
If it is asked: "Is it then the case that these ten stages are utilized by the One Vehicle and entered by the Three Vehicles?
Does this mean that the One Vehicle also establishes the ten stages of common practice?
The answer is as follows:
The One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching is established in terms of wisdom;
the application of the One Vehicle of the Shared Teaching is established in terms of the direct capacity for the Separate Teaching,
because those of the Small Vehicle do not possess the One Vehicle.
The ten stages of common practice (*sādhāraṇa-daśabhūmi*) are not established as that which is employed by the One Vehicle of the same teaching; rather,
they are established for those of inferior capacity who are led [to the higher teaching] by means of the lower teachings.
Since all are impelled by the One Vehicle,
one should reflect upon how, according to this principle, there are the ten stages of common practice (*sādhāraṇa-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, according to another method, Master Daobiao took the Buddha’s Tripiṭaka as his teacher.
Within this Tripiṭaka, the established school that universally adheres to the Mahāyāna and clarifies the principle of the True Mind as the Tathāgatagarbha is regarded as the ultimate.
Therefore, this [system] encompasses the *Laṅkāvatāra*, the *Ratnaketudhāraṇī* (Renwang), and the *Avataṃsaka*.
Taking the three vehicles and six consciousnesses of the distinct teaching (*biejiao*) as its guiding principle,
one cultivates the path until attaining Buddhahood and then returns to enter the universal teaching (*tongjiao*).

The commentary explains:

This is the skillful means (*upāya*) for the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa*), and is thus called "birth-and-death as skillful means" (*upāya-jarāmaraṇa*).
Therefore, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states:

The "birth-and-death of skillful means" refers to the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), which can produce new outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*), just as ignorance produces volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

Just as within the three realms, afflictions and karma are the expedient causes and conditions for the birth-and-death of discrete segments,
they are also termed "segmented birth-and-death.

Suffering and its origin are collectively termed "birth and death" (saṃsāra).

Next, regarding the second [point], it concerns the eighth stage (*bhūmi*).
As for the fact that only the third, fourth, and fifth stages are mentioned while omitting the first seven stages from the first [point],
this is because the sequence of earlier and later has been abbreviated here.
Speaking in terms of reality,
the first [supernormal power] extends through the first seven stages,
while the second belongs exclusively to the eighth stage.
The third is the ninety-second stage.
Furthermore, the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra* states:
"The first is called the body born from the enjoyment of the bliss of samādhi."
Now, according to the *Foxing lun* (Treatise on the Buddha-nature),
Master Paramārtha’s commentary on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* explains the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) as follows:
These are the noble ones of the three vehicles' lineage who,
having entered the first stage (*bhūmi*) and above, receive a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*); therefore,
they are called the "three types."
This does not refer to the three kinds of mind-made bodies, such as those of the bliss of samādhi, mentioned in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"That which possesses birth and death refers to the mind-made bodies of these three kinds of noble ones."
Those who are without birth and death are the final bodies produced by the intentions of these three kinds of noble ones;
according to the Liang commentary, from the eighth stage upward, there is "existence-with-existence" birth and death.
The Bodhisattva Vajra is free from birth and death.
Since both types of birth and death are said in the *Buddhatva-śāstra* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) to pertain to the three kinds of noble ones,
we know that those of the three vehicles’ lineage undergo birth-and-death with existence (*bhava-bhava*) from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward.
They are named according to their original lineage as Arhats,
Pratyekabuddhas, and Greatly Powerful Bodhisattvas; thus,
the seventh fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
Mahāmati, because the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas among the bodhisattvas of the eighth stage are intoxicated by their attachment to the gate of the bliss of the samādhi of cessation,
they are unable to understand it well.
It is solely by ceasing the obstacles caused by the habitual tendencies of the particular and universal characteristics of views that one perceives the view of the selflessness of persons; therefore,
the discriminating mind itself is termed nirvana.
Yet they are unable to know that all phenomena are quiescent.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, you have spoken of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."

The Tathāgata later taught that entering the gate of the bliss of cessation in the eighth stage is something that śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not understand, for it is merely the conceptualization of their own minds.
It is stated later:
"The śrāvakas attain the selflessness of persons but do not attain the emptiness of the selflessness of phenomena.
If it is explained in this way...
Even Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are not yet able to realize the dharmas of the first stage,
let alone the gate of the bliss of cessation in the eighth stage.
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
There are two kinds of śrāvakas.

Regarding what is called the "gate of quiescence in the eightfold eightfold stages," this refers to those who were previously practitioners of the bodhisattva path but subsequently followed the stage of the śrāvaka.
Returning to their original mind, they cultivate the bodhisattva practices and enter together into the gate of quiescence of the eighth stage;
they are not śrāvakas of quiescence characterized by overweening pride,
for the latter are unable to enter the bodhisattva practices.
They have never realized that the three realms are mind-only;
they have never practiced the various dharmas of a bodhisattva;
and they have never practiced the perfections or the conduct of the ten stages.
Therefore, those śrāvakas who have attained definitive cessation cannot realize that gate of the bliss of cessation practiced by bodhisattvas.
Question:
For what reason is it given the name "birth-and-death" (saṃsāra)?
Answer:
That which is termed "transformation-death" (pariṇāmi-cyuti) refers to the process of transformation and alteration,
whether in birth or in death.
Both of these are designated according to their characteristics;
specifically, they are termed "expedient means" (upāya) and "causal conditions" (pratyaya).
These two are distinguished in terms of their function.
The existence of existence and the non-existence of existence are designated as such in contrast to what follows;
thus, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states:
"There is the existence of existence, as in the case of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the upper realms, such as the Anāgāmin."
One who attains parinirvāṇa in the second birth is called "possessing existence" (bhava-bhavin) because one birth remains;
this state of no further birth-and-death is the final body of the transformation-death (pariṇāma-maraṇa).
Therefore, there is once again no birth and death;
thus it is called "non-existence.
Question:
How is this determined according to the stages?
Answer:
If one is categorized by sudden enlightenment, from the eighth stage upward, one undergoes the birth of transformation (*parināmiki-jāti*).
Because from this point upward, afflictions do not arise and there is no possibility of further undergoing birth in discrete segments (*paricchinna-jāti*),
those who attain awakening gradually continue to undergo transformation and rebirth (*pariṇāmi-jāti*) up to and including the seventh stage.
If one speaks in terms of the four types according to their general application, they exist in every stage; however,
if one relies on the specific distinctions of the stages, following only the Liang dynasty treatise,
among the twenty-two instances of ignorance that induce eleven coarse retributions:
In the first eight [stages], one experiences four types of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*) due to the absence of the moon;
these constitute the birth-and-death of skillful means (*upāya*).
Thus, it is known that the stage of skillful means precedes the [next] four stages.
Next, the six types of ignorance induce three kinds of grossness (*dauṣthulya*);
this is the dependent origination of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, it is known that the causal conditions reside in the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages.
Next, the six types of ignorance induce three kinds of coarse heaviness (*dausthulya*);
this constitutes the existence of existence (*bhava-bhava*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
Thus, one should know that the existence of existence resides in the eighth, ninth, and tenth stages.
Next, the two types of ignorance induce a single *dausthulya* (dysfunction).
Since this constitutes the absence of birth and death (*saṃsāra*),
one knows that this absence is the stage of the diamond-like concentration (*vajrāvasthā*).
If these are skillful means and causal conditions, there is birth and death, which arise from their own stage and are severed within their own stage;
if there is no obstruction of birth and death, it is the diamond-like severance of the Buddha-stage.
The reason for this is that the ten stages (daśabhūmi) belong to the stage of training (śaikṣa), and thus the obstacles of each stage are severed by that very stage;
whereas the Buddha-stage belongs to the stage beyond training (aśaikṣa), and thus the obstacles of the Buddha-stage are severed by the diamond-like samādhi (vajropama-samādhi).
Question: If,
as previously stated, these skillful means and conditions are actually the skillful means and conditions for transformation (pariṇāma) rather than actual birth-and-death (saṃsāra),
why is it said in all cases that the retribution of coarse heaviness (dausthulya) they induce is "transformation"?
Answer:
If one is in the stage of expedient causes and conditions for gradual enlightenment, it is termed "segmented" and is called the retribution of heavy afflictions (*dausthulya*).
If viewed from the perspective of what follows, the first four stages are identical to those of ordinary worldlings.
When ignorance is predominant, it serves as the expedient means for the transformation-death (parināmi-cyuti) from the eighth stage upward;
in the fifth, sixth, and seventh stages, one is similar to the two vehicles and to bodhisattvas who have newly begun their practice.
The cultivation of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) also serves as an auxiliary cause for the transformation-body (*pariṇāmi-śarīra*) induced from the eighth stage and above.
Regarding the latter two types [of transformation], which constitute the actual substance of the transformation,
Master Huiyuan says:
It is taught that there are six layers for each of the two types of birth and death.
Regarding what are called the six layers of the *pariccheda* (segmented) birth and death,
these consist of three layers of the evil realms and three layers of the good realms.
Question:
What are the three levels of the evil realms?
Answer:
First, the segmented evil karma experienced by ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) serves as the cause,
and the four stages of abiding (*catur-vāsabhūmi*) serve as the condition.
Second, the segmented evil karma experienced by those who have attained the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) serves as the cause.
The four stages of abiding (*catur-vihāra-bhūmi*) serve as the conditions;
compassion and vows act as the auxiliary support;
and the various types of segmented karmic retribution (*bheda-karma*) received from the three natures upward, up to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), serve as the cause.
Compassionate vows serve as the primary condition;
the four stages of abiding (catur-vihāra-bhūmi) act as auxiliary supports.
Based on these three layers, the segmented existence of the evil realms is established.
Question:
What are the three levels of the wholesome realms (sugati) regarding their segmentation?
Answer:
First, the segmented wholesome karma received by ordinary beings, the followers of the two vehicles, and those in the stage of the ten faiths of the Mahāyāna serves as the cause;
the four abiding grounds serve as the condition.
Second, the segmented wholesome karma received by those of the two natures during the stage of understanding and practice serves as the cause.
The four stages of abiding (catur-vihāra-bhūmi) serve as the primary conditions;
compassion and vows act as auxiliary supports;
and the fragmented wholesome karma acquired from the three higher stages serves as the cause.
Compassionate vows serve as the primary condition;
the four stages of abiding (catur-vihāra-bhūmi) serve as auxiliary support.
Based on these three layers, one defines the "segmented" nature of the wholesome path.
Regarding what is called the sixfold transformation-death (*pariṇāma-maraṇa*):
there are three layers of the objective consciousness (*vastu-vijñāna*) and three layers of the deluded consciousness (*mṛṣā-vijñāna*).
Question:
Question: How do the three layers of transformation of the event-consciousness (*vṛtti-vijñāna*) occur?
Answer:
First, for Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, the transformation of the event-consciousness they undergo takes the contemplation of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-darśana*) as its cause.
With the ground of abiding ignorance as the condition,

the contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena within the transformational consciousness experienced by those of the two types of natures during the stage of practice through understanding serves as the direct cause;
with the ground of abiding ignorance as the condition.

The understanding of the signless, which is neither existent nor non-existent, within the *pariṇāma-vijñāna* experienced on the three stages [of the bodhisattva] serves as the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*),
while the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) serves as the condition (*pratyaya*).
With respect to these three layers, they are established within the *vastu-vijñāna*.
What are the three levels of transformation and rebirth?
Answer:
First, within the deluded consciousness experienced prior to the [first] stage.
All false conceptualizations take true contemplation as their cause and the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) as their condition.
Within the midst of the deluded consciousness of the transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*) experienced from the eighth stage upward...
Taking only the true and devoid of delusion as the correct cause by means of the cessation of conceptualization and observation,
and taking the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*) as the condition—
based on these three layers, there are three layers of transformative birth-and-death (*pariṇāma-cyuti*) within deluded consciousness.

"If one follows the Final Teaching (zhōngjiào), prior to the stages [of the bodhisattva path], one retains the afflictions to undergo the body of segmented birth;

this cites the fifth section, the "Chapter on the Time of Cultivation," from the eleventh fascicle of that treatise.

If one perceives suchness, one enters the stage of pure mental conduct (*śuddhāśayacarī-bhūmi*).
This name applies equally from the first stage through the tenth stage.

The first is named according to the Path, namely, the practice of pure mental activity (*śuddhamanaskāra*). The latter three are named according to their specific characteristics:

up to the seventh bhūmi, they practice without signs but with effortful application.

once the eighth stage is fully perfected, their signless practice in the eighth stage has become effortlessly accomplished.
On the ninth and tenth stages, the practice of signlessness (*animitta*) and effortlessness (*anābhoga*) is not yet perfected;
it is only at the end of the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa that this signless and effortless state is finally accomplished.

If there are only these three stages, how are they established as five?

the *kulaṃkula* (one who goes from family to family) is the second person.
The Sakṛdāgāmin is the third person;
the Ekabījī is the fourth person;
and the Anāgāmin is the fifth person.

the first stage constitutes the first position;
from the second stage through the seventh stage constitutes the second position.

these may also be established as five types of persons.

The answer is as stated by Huijing: "The Mirror of Wisdom."

those who are persons of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*) are so designated because they share the same category as those on the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
Regarding those who go from family to family:
these are those who, having died among humans, are reborn in the heavens,
and then return once more to the human realm.
Because one goes from family to family, it is called "family-to-family.
In the second stage (*bhūmi*), one practices by means of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) while abandoning the afflictions;
upon reaching the fourth stage, one again attains that same untainted wisdom.

because it is exclusively the stage of effortful application (*sābhoga*), it is based on the principle that one undergoes only half a birth.
From the eighth stage upward, one is free from effortful application (*anābhoga*).
Therefore, it may be understood by analogy with those who have already transcended desire.

the dialogue states:
If one relies on the Final Teaching of the Three Vehicles, then all sentient beings without exception will attain Buddhahood,

"If it is the place where one attains Buddhahood..."

in the Final Teaching, there are no separate [stages].

the lower fascicle states:
Thus, the lineage (gotra) is established within the very nature of suchness (tathatā).
Consequently, all sentient beings without exception possess this nature.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
White stone has the nature of silver;
yellow stone has the nature of gold;
water has the nature of moisture.
Fire is characterized by heat.
All sentient beings possess the nature of nirvana,
because there is no deluded consciousness that cannot return to its own true nature.
As the sutra says: "Sentient beings are likewise;
they all possess a mind.
All who possess a mind will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
For this reason, I have always proclaimed that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.

As it is said in an objection:

Although the Buddha possesses a mind, it is not something to be attained [anew].
Likewise, although sentient beings who lack intrinsic nature possess minds, these too are not things to be attained [anew].
Answer:
The sūtra itself has already distinguished [the case] from such confusion;
therefore, it simply says that sentient beings possess a mind,
and does not say the Buddha does.
Because they undergo birth in various places, they are called sentient beings;
thus, they are not the same as the Buddha.

Mañjuśrī, all sentient beings are of one single characteristic;

According to the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), all sentient beings— both those in the provisional and the ultimate [teachings]— equally attain Buddhahood,
as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Based on this principle, the preceding four propositions are understood as the One Vehicle’s common teaching (*sādhāraṇa-deśanā*), not its distinct teaching (*asādhāraṇa-deśanā*).
As for the period before and after attaining Buddhahood:
In every moment of thought, they attain Buddhahood, exhausting all sentient beings to be converted;
throughout all stages—
from the ten abodes onwards until the attainment of Bodhi— they exhaust the entire realm of sentient beings.
The state of accomplishment is all-pervasive and without before or after,
for it constitutes a single tree of dependent origination.
As for the time of attaining Buddhahood:
According to the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), the timing of attaining Buddhahood is in all cases indefinite;
this is because the temporal conditions differ across the worlds of the ten directions.
The "Indra-world" and others are all established according to their respective positions within the stage of retribution.
Because it is taught that conditioned kalpas have characteristics such as mutual formation and mutual inclusion,
there is no fixed duration;
yet this does not contradict the principle of time.
The final fascicle states:
"All temporal divisions are entirely indeterminate. Why is this so?"
Because all kalpas interpenetrate one another;
because their characteristics are identical;
and because they universally pervade all worlds such as those of Indra.
Nevertheless, each occurs according to its own circumstances—
whether in a single thought-moment or over immeasurable eons— and thus does not contravene the law of time.
The *Kongmu* (Comprehensive Overview), Part IV, states:
If the meaning of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) is such that it spans inexhaustible eons,
on what basis can one rely upon the One Vehicle?
[For] all sentient beings would have already attained Buddhahood, yet they would continue to newly attain Buddhahood for the sake of sentient beings.
Nor does one attain perfect enlightenment while remaining on the stage of training;
since this is not limited by time,
it is therefore inexhaustible.
This teaching of the meaning and the salvific measure gives rise to faith in the virtues of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Furthermore, the numerical dharmas are common to the virtues of the ten stages.
As for the Buddhas of other directions who appear through transformation (*nirmāṇa*):
If one relies on the One Vehicle (ekayāna), there are only ten Buddhas;
this is explained according to their activities without distinguishing between those produced through cultivation and those that are originally existent.
If one realizes the essence of the Great Way, that essence is itself all-encompassing (sarvākāra).
The essence and characteristics are the manifestations of all aspects;
the function is the operation of all aspects.
The Buddhas appearing in all directions—whether in name or in meaning—all manifest through the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*) of Śākyamuni; there is no other Buddha.
If one relies on the One Vehicle as the Mother of all Buddhas,
then all Buddhas abide within the ocean-seal samādhi-power of Śākyamuni Buddha;
by this principle, it should be understood that all their retinues and so forth are likewise the same.
The meanings of essence, characteristic, and function, as well as transformations and modifications of nature, should be understood accordingly.
As for the mutual entry and mutual functioning of the emotional faculties,
according to the teaching of the One Vehicle, both transformations and modifications of nature are based upon dependent origination.
This Dharma-manifestation likewise possesses no distinct nature that can be transformed or altered.
Whether it is the manifestation itself or the act of acting, both are subsumed within the aforementioned transformation.
Nevertheless, the essence of the One Vehicle possesses both the ordinary body of sentient beings and its inherent virtuous qualities.
Regarding the differentiation of cause and effect:

if one relies on the limits and full extent of all causes and effects for attaining Buddhahood within the One Vehicle, this universally encompasses the limits of all realms, including those that are Indra-like, secret, and subtle.
It exhausts the limits and measure of the three periods of time,
according to the "Universal Good Gate" (*Samantabhadramukha*) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
All aspects of practice, such as the severing of delusions, encompass both the causal and resultant stages, exhausting them all without exception.
If one attains Buddhahood by cultivating the path, according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teaching, this applies to all preceding capacities.
If it is necessary to attain Buddhahood, one may do so repeatedly; each time, one attains Buddhahood by newly severing the fetters (saṃyojana).
Nor does one attain Buddhahood by abiding in the stage of awakening;
if one encounters beings who are not yet ready for enlightenment, one remains eternally unenlightened,
just like the great ocean.
Among all stages, there is no overflowing;
this refers to the *icchantika* bodhisattva mentioned in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
When confronted with the diverse capacities of different ailments, there is neither success nor failure.
If it refers to Samantabhadra, then it is both established and unestablished.
If it refers to the physical form of the Buddha,
then according to the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) teaching, these are his virtues and marks.
This is not a matter of affirming virtue and negating characteristics; rather,
it is because the principle of dependent origination fully encompasses the meanings of both the direct and reverse orders, as well as what is performed and what is not performed.
The physical basis (*āśraya*) for the stages of the lineage and its practice is as explained in the subsequent fascicle.

Section Four: The Gate of the Lineage for Swiftly Attaining Buddhahood. The fourth topical outline (*koṭu-mok*) states: Section Four: The Gate of the Lineage for Swiftly Attaining Buddhahood. It says:
Furthermore, regarding the statement that what the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas awakened to over immeasurable kalpas according to the text of Maitreya,
Sudhana attained in a single lifetime,
this is based on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
There are five ways to swiftly attain Buddhahood.
First, by relying on a superior body, one proceeds from the stage of seeing and hearing;
after one more birth, upon reaching the concentration free from defilement (*vimala-samādhi*), one attains Buddhahood in that final body.
Second, based on seeing and hearing, one swiftly attains realization;
third, based on a single moment, one swiftly attains Buddhahood;
fourth, based on a single thought-moment, one swiftly attains Buddhahood.
Fifth, by relying on non-conceptualization (*amanasikāra*), one swiftly attains the state of Buddhahood.
Regarding the first meaning, there are four points as explained above.
Second, regarding those who attain swift realization by relying on seeing and hearing [the teachings]:
As in the case of the first bhūmi, there are three periods of benefit:
first, the benefit at the time of hearing;
second, the benefit at the time of practice.
Third is the benefit at the time of rebirth.
Therefore, the *Dilun* states:
"All these Tathāgatas bestow their protective empowerment upon all bodhisattvas."
This person is able to hear and uphold such a subtle and sublime Dharma;
this is the benefit at the time of hearing.
All stages are pure and stainless.
Gradually fulfilling [these qualities],
one realizes the ten powers of a Buddha and attains unsurpassed enlightenment;
this is the benefit during the time of practice.
Even if one were in the midst of the great ocean or within the fires at the end of an eon, if they possess resolute faith and are free from doubt, they will certainly hear this sutra;
this is its further benefit.
Bodhisattvas on the stages of intention, faith, and practice who hear and uphold this sublime Dharma spoken by Vajragarbha [shall likewise attain it].
One immediately receives the empowerment of all Buddhas and becomes free from all demonic activities.
This is the benefit at the time of hearing; having heard this supreme Dharma, one gradually cultivates and fulfills the practices of the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
This continues until the attainment of bodhi;
this is called the benefit during the time of practice.
Furthermore, there are sentient beings whose destinies are not fixed.
Having heard this subtle and wondrous Dharma of the Ten Grounds, they plant the seed of the vajra;
though they may be born in the happy realms, the evil destinies, or difficult places for many kalpas,
within those difficult places they will inevitably encounter this very sutra.
This is called the benefit at the time of rebirth.
